sections.h2: Where does a Washington County, PA deed get recorded?
sections.html:
At the Recorder of Deeds office in the Crossroads Center, 95 W. Beau St., Suite 520, Washington, PA 15301. The phone number is 724-228-6806. Doors are open from 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., but the office stops taking documents for recording at 4:00 p.m.

The office dates from 1781, the same year the county itself was carved out of Westmoreland County. By its own description it records deeds, mortgages and subdivision plans, collects the fees and taxes that come with them, and passes the money on to the state, the county, the municipalities and the school districts. Recorded documents are indexed, verified and scanned within the same business day.

For a seller in Washington County, this office is the last stop on a sale. The deed is signed at closing, then recorded here, and the recording is what puts the buyer's name into the public record. Anyone who wants to check what is already on file for a property can search online: every deed from 1781 to the present is available through Landex, and the office keeps public computers for walk-in searches.

sections.h2: What does the Washington County recorder charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
The base fee depends on document type, and every base fee already covers four pages, four indexed names and one PIN. The county posts a fee schedule and a fee calculator on the recorder page, so check the current figure there before you write a check.

Washington County recorder charges on top of the base fee, from the county recorder page
ItemCharge
Included in the base fee4 pages, 4 indexed names, 1 PIN
Each additional page$2.00
Each additional indexed name$0.50
Each additional PIN$10.00
Court-related surcharge (CJEA) after the fiscal code changeUp from $2.50 to $3.50, a $1 increase

The county explains that the printed schedule lags behind the $1 CJEA increase, so a recent schedule on the site may show a figure $1 lower than what the counter collects. If the total is unclear, the office asks you to call 724-228-6806 rather than guess.

Two small details catch people out. The PIN charge applies per parcel number, so a sale that combines several parcels costs more than a single-lot sale. And the extra-page charge adds up on long documents, such as a deed that carries a full legal description and several exhibits.

sections.h2: Who pays realty transfer tax on a Washington County sale?
sections.html:
The buyer and the seller share liability. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue states that the commonwealth tax is 1 percent of the value transferred and that grantor and grantee are held jointly and severally liable, which means the state can collect the full amount from either one.

County recorders collect that state share, often together with a local transfer tax, and then forward it. Washington County's recorder page says it distributes receipts to the state, county, municipalities and school districts, so the local rate depends on where the house sits. Ask the Recorder of Deeds, or your closing agent, for the combined rate that applies to your municipality before you price the sale.

  • Some transfers are exempt, including certain transfers between family members, transfers to government units and property that passes by will or intestate succession.
  • A claimed exemption normally has to be documented, so ask the office which form to attach.
  • The cost of the tax is usually settled in the sale contract, not by the recorder.

sections.h2: What formatting rules can get a Washington County document rejected?
sections.html:
Page size and type size are the two that the county stresses on its recorder page. The office no longer accepts legal-size pages electronically, and it sets minimum fonts: 12 point on letter-size pages and 14 point on legal-size pages.

Subdivision plans follow their own rules. They are filed on paper or mylar, and they need signatures from the Washington County Planning Commission, the local planning commission where one applies, the board of supervisors or borough council, and the owners of the land being divided. The plan also carries an engineer's seal, and it has to be recorded within 90 days of the local governing body's approval.

  • Check page size before you scan a deed for e-recording.
  • Confirm the type size on a long exhibit, since small print is a common reason for a bounce.
  • For a plan, count the 90 days from the local approval, not from the date you finish the drawings.

sections.h2: What is Washington County like for a house sale?
sections.html:
It is a mid-sized, mostly owner-occupied county south of Pittsburgh. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page shows 210,802 residents in 2025 across 857 square miles of land, 99,340 housing units and 88,505 households in the 2020 to 2024 survey.

Of occupied homes, 76.1 percent are lived in by their owners. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $228,500, median gross rent is $949, and median household income is $78,958. Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,618.

The county seat is the city of Washington, and the only other city is Monongahela. Canonsburg and Charleroi are among the larger boroughs, and Peters Township is the largest municipality. Washington & Jefferson College sits in the city of Washington, and the county's economy leans on coal and on the Southpointe business park, which covers more than 800 acres. Winters are cold: the county averages about 37.8 inches of snow a year, mostly between November and April, which matters for roofs, gutters and furnaces when a buyer inspects an older house.

sections.h2: Which school districts and towns shape buyer demand in Washington County?
sections.html:
Districts such as Canon-McMillan, Peters Township, Charleroi, Burgettstown Area and Chartiers-Houston each pull a different pool of buyers. The county has many small districts, so two houses a few miles apart can sit in separate districts with separate tax bills.

That is why a Washington County sale is easier to price when the listing names the district. Peters Township, in the northeast corner near Allegheny County, is the county's largest municipality, while the Mon Valley boroughs along the river, including Charleroi, are older and more affordable. The median home in the Census data is valued at $228,500, but the spread across these communities is wide.

sections.h2: What if the house has unpaid taxes before the deed is recorded?
sections.html:
Washington County splits the work between two offices. The Treasurer collects county taxes at 95 W. Beau St., Suite 130, hours 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., phone 724-228-6780. The Tax Revenue Department, at Suite 525 and 724-228-6850, handles assessments and delinquent claims.

The Treasurer's page says personal checks have not been accepted for delinquent taxes since October 6, 2025. Accepted payment is certified check, money order, cash or card. Online payments carry a fee: 2.50 percent with a $2.00 minimum for credit or debit cards, or $1.50 for an electronic check.

If a back-tax balance is attached to the property, get a written payoff figure from the Tax Revenue Department before closing so the amount can be paid out of the sale. The county also has a Board of Assessment Appeals, and Tax Revenue can explain how an appeal is filed.

faqs.q: What time does the Washington County recorder stop accepting deeds?
faqs.a: Recording stops at 4:00 p.m., even though the office stays open until 4:30 p.m. The office is at 95 W. Beau St., Suite 520, in Washington, and a deed that arrives after 4:00 p.m. waits for the next business day.

faqs.q: Can I record a legal-size deed electronically in Washington County?
faqs.a: No. The county says it no longer accepts legal-size pages electronically. Letter-size pages need at least 12 point type and legal-size pages need at least 14 point, so bring a paper original if the document is on legal paper.

faqs.q: Does a Washington County deed fee cover extra pages and names?
faqs.a: The base fee covers four pages, four indexed names and one PIN. Each page beyond four costs $2.00, each extra name $0.50 and each extra PIN $10.00, and the county added $1 to its CJEA surcharge, so confirm the total by phone at 724-228-6806.

faqs.q: How can I look up recorded deeds in Washington County, PA?
faqs.a: Use Landex online, which holds deeds from 1781 to the present, or use the public computers inside the Recorder of Deeds office. Landex support is 1-800-370-2836, option 4, according to the county page.

faqs.q: Who owes the transfer tax when a Washington County house sells?
faqs.a: Both sides are liable. Pennsylvania imposes 1 percent on the value transferred and holds buyer and seller jointly responsible, and a local tax is usually added. Your sale contract decides who actually pays, and the recorder can confirm the local rate.
